svg.aria-label: Diagram: Microsoft Entra ID Protection risk lifecycle, showing the risk state machine from At risk to Remediated, Dismissed or Confirmed compromised and who closes each, the distinction between dismissing a risk and confirming a user safe, the effect each administrator verb has on the machine learning model, the five token theft detections that are no longer auto-remediated, and the retirement of the legacy risk policies on 1 October 2026
svg.title: A risk is a state machine, and the only interesting question is who closes it
svg.text: A risk is a state machine. The only interesting question is who closes it, and how.
Post #42 covered what gets detected. This is what happens next — and the state it lands in is a durable claim about the account.
Every risk starts At risk. Five ways out, and they do not mean the same thing.
CLOSED BY
ENDS AS
RISK DETAIL RECORDED
User passes MFA
Remediated
“User passed multifactor authentication”
User changes password
Remediated
“User performed secured password reset”
Entra reassesses it
Dismissed
“Microsoft Entra ID Protection assessed sign-in safe”
Admin clicks Dismiss
Dismissed
“Admin dismissed all risk for user” — and nothing changed
Admin confirms breach
Confirmed compromised
sets user risk to high, and adds a detection of its own
Dismissed does not mean safe
“Because this method doesn’t change the user’s existing
password, it doesn’t bring their identity back into a safe
state.”
The report goes quiet. The credential is untouched.
Dismiss is for a benign true positive — a pen test, an
approved tool. It says “real, but not malicious”, and
similar activity keeps being evaluated.
Three verbs, three different effects on the model
Confirm compromised
true positive — risk to high, new detection added
Confirm safe
false positive — “removes risk and detections on this user
and places it in learning mode to relearn”
Dismiss
benign true positive — the detection was right, the
activity was fine, keep detecting it
Token theft detections stopped auto-remediating
“We no longer autoremediate sessions with MFA claims when a token theft related or the Verified threat actor IP detection
triggers during sign-in.” Five of them: Microsoft Entra threat intelligence · Anomalous token · Attacker in the Middle ·
Verified threat actor IP · Token issuer anomaly.
The reasoning is the whole of posts #39 and #40: an MFA claim in a stolen token is the attacker’s MFA claim. Passing it proves
nothing. These now require a secure password change and reauthentication to clear.
Require risk remediation adapts to how the user signs in
Password user, leaked credential
secure password change, then “their previous sessions are revoked”
Passwordless user, no password involved
sessions revoked, prompted to sign in again — nothing to change
Attacker added a device
“The Entra device object is disabled, blocking new token issuance”
Precedence, when policies overlap: Require risk remediation beats Require password change; Block beats everything.
Not available for external and guest users, because session revocation is not supported for them.
A date: the legacy risk policies retire on 1 October 2026
If the user risk or sign-in risk policy is still configured inside ID Protection rather than Conditional Access, it stops. Moving them
buys report-only mode, Graph, sign-in frequency, and risk combined with location — all the things posts #41 to #43 depended on.
And the licence cliff is unusually steep: on P1, Risky sign-ins shows “Limited Information. No risk detail or risk level is shown.”
Sources: ID Protection risk-based access policies, Remediate risks and unblock users, What is ID Protection, and Provide risk feedback, on Microsoft Learn.
